claim: MemSkill argues that memory extraction, consolidation, and pruning should be reframed as learnable, evolvable 'skills' rather than fixed hand-designed operations, and that this improves agent task performance over strong baselines while generalizing across settings.
method: A controller learns to select a small set of relevant memory skills per situation, an LLM-based executor applies the selected skills to produce memories, and a periodically-run designer reviews hard cases where selected skills yielded incorrect or incomplete memories to propose refinements or new skills, forming a closed loop that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself.
evidence: Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld; the paper states MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings, but no specific headline accuracy numbers are given in the provided text.
stated_limitations: Near-verbatim (source notes exact wording not retrieved): the designer relies on LLM prompting to diagnose hard cases and generate/refine skills, carrying a risk of misdiagnosis; the framework incurs training/adaptation overhead from repeated LLM calls for the executor and periodic designer review; memory access at query time still relies on a predefined (e.g., dense) retrieval strategy rather than a learned one, so retrieval behavior remains largely fixed even as memory content becomes more adaptive.
not_tested: No head-to-head numbers isolating how much improvement comes from the skill-based write/consolidation policy versus retrieval; no reported interaction between skill evolution and prompt/instruction optimization.
title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents

claim: ReMe claims that treating procedural memory as an actively refined, lifecycle-managed system rather than a static append-only archive achieves state-of-the-art agent memory performance and produces a memory-scaling effect in which a smaller model with memory outperforms a larger memoryless model.
method: Three mechanisms across the memory lifecycle: multi-faceted distillation (extracting fine-grained experiences from success patterns, failure triggers, and comparative insights), context-adaptive reuse (tailoring historical insights to new contexts via scenario-aware indexing), and utility-based refinement (autonomously adding valid memories and pruning outdated ones to keep a compact, high-quality experience pool).
evidence: Experiments on BFCL-V3 and AppWorld; Qwen3-8B equipped with ReMe outperforms larger, memoryless Qwen3-14B; no other specific headline numbers are stated in the provided text.
not_tested: No paper-stated limitations were available to assess; beyond the single Qwen3-8B vs. Qwen3-14B comparison, no other quantitative head-to-head numbers or ablations are given in the provided text.
title: Remember Me, Refine Me: A Dynamic Procedural Memory Framework for Experience-Driven Agent Evolution

claim: This survey argues that AI research is entering a 'second half' centered on real-world utility in long-horizon, dynamic agentic settings, and that memory is the critical substrate through which agents self-evolve, offering a unified taxonomy of agent memory along substrate, cognitive mechanism, and subject dimensions, plus an account of how memory management itself is becoming a trainable capability.
method: A survey/taxonomy: organizes foundation agent memory along memory substrate (internal parametric vs. external retrieval-augmented stores), cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural), and memory subject (user-centric personalization vs. agent-centric experience); analyzes memory operation under single- and multi-agent topologies; reviews learning policies over memory operations and evaluation benchmarks/metrics.
evidence: A literature survey covering, per the abstract, hundreds of papers released in 2025 on agent memory; reviews evaluation benchmarks and metrics for memory utility rather than running new experiments itself.
stated_limitations: Managing memory dynamics across intra-task and cross-task timescales is a fundamental open challenge: intra-task, agents must decide what to retain/compress/discard from heterogeneous streams under context-window constraints; cross-task, current approaches emphasize inference-time reuse over principled consolidation and generalization; establishing a unified framework connecting classical continual learning objectives with structured memory design remains a key open direction. (Source notes the survey lists six open challenges total but only this one was retrievable in detail.)
not_tested: As a survey it runs no controlled experiments of its own comparing memory designs, so it provides no direct quantitative/causal evidence for any specific memory mechanism; the full enumerated list of open challenges beyond the one quoted is not available.
title: A Survey of Agent Memory in the Second Half: Towards Self-Evolving and Long-Horizon Agents

claim: ZERA proposes a framework that jointly optimizes both system and user prompts through principled, low-overhead refinement, enabling fast convergence to high-quality prompts using minimal examples and short iteration cycles.
method: Prompts are scored using eight generalizable criteria with automatically inferred weights, and revised based on the resulting structured critiques, jointly refining system and user prompts together.
evidence: Evaluated across five LLMs and nine diverse datasets spanning reasoning, summarization, and code generation tasks; reports consistent improvements over strong baselines and ablations showing each component's contribution, but no specific headline numbers are given in the provided text.
stated_limitations: ZERA's evaluation on summarization tasks relies entirely on automatic metrics (e.g., ROUGE-L) without human judgment, which may overlook nuances like coherence or factuality. Additionally, although ZERA is designed to operate with minimal supervision, it still requires a small number of training samples (typically 5-20) for each task to perform its principle-based optimization.
not_tested: No human evaluation of summarization quality is performed; the paper does not test interaction of its optimized prompts with an external memory bank or experience store.
title: ZERA: Zero-init Instruction Evolving Refinement Agent - From Zero Instructions to Structured Prompts via Principle-based Optimization

claim: The paper reports a previously unreported phenomenon, the Prompt Optimization Coupling Effect (POCE): when multiple stochastic optimization signals (episodic memory, multi-objective Pareto selection, adaptive evaluation) operate within a closed reflective loop, they interact to simultaneously improve performance and amplify variance in ways not predictable from analyzing the components in isolation.
method: MAGE (Memory-Augmented Goal-directed Prompt Evolution) is presented as a controlled ablation platform, not a superior optimizer in absolute terms, integrating episodic memory, multi-objective Pareto selection, and adaptive evaluation to study component interaction in iterative prompt optimization.
evidence: On gpt-4o-mini with 5 seeds: MAGE achieves 46.4% vs. GEPA's 34.0% on GSM8K-Hard (+12.4%, P(MAGE>GEPA)=0.998), with comparable variance (7.3% vs. 7.0%); expanding the candidate pool from n=3 to n=5 improves mean accuracy by +21.6% while increasing variance by 3.7x; further validated on Llama 3.1 8B, where variance amplification disappears once the base model already achieves high accuracy; failure-grounded reflection is essential, as score-only (OPRO) or abstract-critique (Self-Refine) methods fail to improve prompts; in low-data regimes (Ntrain=30) well-designed fixed prompts outperform all reflective optimizers.
stated_limitations: Closely paraphrased (verbatim section not retrievable): cross-task interference is a key limitation because retrieval uses Jaccard word-overlap, so BBH optimization can retrieve GSM8K arithmetic traces carrying little useful/semantic signal; for production use the authors recommend task-type filtering or a dense retrieval method (e.g., a frozen sentence-transformer encoder such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with FAISS); in low-data settings optimized prompts can underperform strong fixed prompts, implying scaffold design often matters more than optimization; the most important future direction is full multi-model validation (e.g., GPT-4o, Mistral-7B) with additional seeds; it is also left open whether MAGE yields additional gains when initialized from already-strong scaffolds (CoT-zero, CoT-math).
not_tested: Full multi-model validation beyond gpt-4o-mini and Llama 3.1 8B is left as future work; dense/semantic retrieval is not tested against the Jaccard word-overlap retrieval actually used; initialization from already-strong scaffolds is left as an open question.
title: MAGE: Understanding Stability-Performance Trade-offs in Multi-component Prompt Optimization

claim: The paper introduces AgentNoiseBench, a framework for systematically evaluating the robustness of tool-using LLM agents under noisy conditions (user-noise and tool-noise), finding that current agentic models show consistent performance variation and sensitivity to realistic environmental perturbations.
method: The authors analyze biases and uncertainties in real-world agent scenarios, categorize environmental noise into user-noise and tool-noise, and build an automated pipeline that injects controllable noise into existing agent-centric benchmarks while preserving task solvability.
evidence: Extensive evaluations across a wide range of models with diverse architectures and parameter scales; no specific benchmark names, model list, or headline numbers are stated in the provided text.
not_tested: No specific benchmark names, models, or quantitative headline results are given in the provided text, so the generality/magnitude of the reported sensitivity cannot be verified from this text; no comparison to memory-based or other mitigation strategies is mentioned.
title: AgentNoiseBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents Under Noisy Condition

claim: The paper proposes Structured Experience Compression (SEC), which distills each trajectory into a compact four-field unit for retrieval-augmented experience replay, claiming it outperforms raw-trajectory retrieval while using far fewer context tokens and degrading more gracefully under noisy or mismatched records.
method: Each trajectory is distilled into a four-field unit encoding task type (T), key decisions (D), failure reason (F), and repair action (R); at inference time the top-k units closest to the current task are retrieved and appended to the prompt.
evidence: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop: SEC outperforms raw-trajectory retrieval by 7.7 percentage points on ALFWorld and by an absolute reward gain of 0.056 on WebShop, while consuming only 37% of the context tokens; also reported to degrade more gracefully when the pool contains noisy or mismatched records.
not_tested: No details are given on the similarity/selection mechanism behind 'top-k closest to the current task' beyond that description; no comparison to learned or dense retrieval methods; no discussion of interaction with prompt optimization.
title: Experience Retrieval Compression for Continual Adaptation of LLM Agents

claim: Agent Memory Distillation (AMD) is a training-free framework that transfers structured knowledge from a large teacher agent to a small student agent via hierarchical memory (Workflow, Subtask, Function), yielding substantial accuracy gains for small student models on tool-use benchmarks.
method: AMD constructs three complementary memory types from successful teacher trajectories: Workflow memory (task-level strategies), Subtask memory (concrete behavioral examples at intermediate granularity), and Function memory (per-function calling conventions and common pitfalls); Workflow and Subtask memories are injected proactively at the start of each task, while Function memory is retrieved reactively upon tool-calling errors.
evidence: Evaluated on three tool-use benchmarks (AppWorld, BFCL V3, ToolSandbox) using four student models (4B-8B parameters) with GPT-5-mini as teacher; achieves average accuracy gains of 27.2 percentage points on AppWorld, 11.2 percentage points on BFCL V3, and 3.4 percentage points on ToolSandbox, outperforming existing memory-based baselines; Subtask memory contributes the largest gains; 4B-sized students benefit most.
stated_limitations: Paraphrased from search results (full verbatim not retrieved): small student models exhibit limited in-context learning ability and weaker instruction-following capacity compared to larger models, causing difficulty effectively interpreting and applying teacher memories even when directly provided; the capability gap between teacher and student models can fundamentally limit distillation effectiveness.
not_tested: No ablation of the proactive injection budget (Workflow+Subtask injected at task start) for size/amount is reported; no interaction between AMD's memory and prompt optimization of student instructions is discussed.
title: Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory

claim: CDMem, a context-dependent memory framework miming human memory processes through multistage encoding, context-aware storage, and retrieval, enables LLM-centric agents to outperform state-of-the-art online approaches on interactive decision-making tasks.
method: Multistage memory encoding (expert encoding of raw trajectories, short-term encoding of current-task experience, long-term encoding of past-task insights) combined with a graph-structured, context-dependent indexing mechanism for storage/retrieval, operating as an online learning architecture that updates memory as it adapts to novel environments.
evidence: ALFWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks using GPT-4o-mini; achieves success rates of 85.8% and 56.0% respectively, surpassing state-of-the-art online LLM-centric approaches.
not_tested: No backbones other than GPT-4o-mini are reported, and no ablation isolating the contribution of the multistage encoding versus the graph-structured retrieval is described.
title: An Efficient Context-Dependent Memory Framework for LLM-Centric Agents

claim: Current automatic agent self-evolution methods do not reliably achieve procedural ability transfer across all agentic domains, scaffolds, and backbones, even though a verified Ability-grounded reference condition does improve held-out performance.
method: EvoAgentBench extracts trace-grounded Abilities from agent executions, canonicalizes them into operational units via a three-judge process with domain-expert review, and builds domain-specific Ability Graphs linking tasks that share procedural overlap, evaluated on a 528/267 train/test split.
evidence: Four agentic domains (web research, algorithmic reasoning, software engineering, knowledge work), two scaffolds, three backbones, per-domain test sets of 56-86 tasks with three runs per cell; the Ability-grounded reference condition improves held-out performance across all four domains, but automatic methods show inconsistent gains and no automatic method sustains positive gain in all settings.
stated_limitations: Evaluated on four long-horizon text-based domains with three open-source construction backbones only, not extended to multimodal/embodied agents or larger/proprietary model families; Ability extraction uses a single LLM so the vocabulary reflects that extractor's idiosyncrasies (mitigated but not eliminated by multi-judge canonicalization); each evaluation cell aggregates only three runs over 56-86 tasks, sufficient for paradigm-level patterns but not finer-grained per-domain analysis; backbones may have seen source-benchmark data during pretraining, which shifts absolute scores though not the condition comparisons the benchmark targets.
not_tested: Multimodal or embodied agents and larger/proprietary model families are not tested, and the effect of alternative Ability extractors on the resulting vocabulary is left as future work.
title: EvoAgentBench: Benchmarking Agent Self-Evolution via Ability Transfer

claim: Reflecting on single-attempt task trajectories to extract transferable heuristics, then selectively retrieving and injecting them into context at test time, enables effective self-improvement in LLM agents.
method: Experiential Reflective Learning (ERL) reflects on task trajectories and outcomes to generate heuristics capturing actionable lessons; at test time, relevant heuristics are retrieved based on the current task and injected into the agent's context to guide execution.
evidence: Gaia2 benchmark; ERL improves success rate by 7.8% over a ReAct baseline with large gains in task completion reliability, and outperforms prior experiential learning methods; ablations show selective retrieval is essential and that heuristics are more transferable than few-shot trajectory prompting.
not_tested: The paper's actual limitations text could not be confirmed as verbatim, and evaluation beyond Gaia2/ReAct comparison (e.g., other benchmarks or backbones) is not reported in the available text.
title: Experiential Reflective Learning for Self-Improving LLM Agents

claim: Outcome-only evaluation of LLM agents' social behavior in mixed-motive games misses substantial differences in social competence that a process-aware, three-view evaluation framework reveals.
method: M3-BENCH, a benchmark of 24 mixed-motive games, combines Behavioral Trajectory Analysis (BTA), Reasoning Process Analysis (RPA), and Communication Content Analysis (CCA) into a process-aware evaluation framework.
evidence: 11 frontier LLMs plus a human baseline; reveals an "overthink-undercommunicate" pattern where reasoning models score well on internal deliberation but fail to communicate effectively; top models surpass humans on task outcomes but humans show markedly higher cross-view consistency; the three-view decomposition surfaces safety-relevant risks such as cooperative behavior paired with latent opportunistic reasoning that outcome-only metrics miss.
not_tested: No memory or prompt-optimization mechanisms are evaluated, and generalization of the findings beyond the 24 games or the 11 models tested is not addressed.
title: M3-BENCH: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agents Social Behaviors in Mixed-Motive Games

claim: Treating memory as an active, self-optimizing component via verifiable write admission, utility-based scheduling, and cross-domain knowledge diffusion improves reasoning accuracy while reducing token overhead compared with strong memory baselines.
method: SEDM integrates verifiable write admission based on reproducible replay, a self-scheduling memory controller that dynamically ranks and consolidates entries by empirical utility, and cross-domain knowledge diffusion that abstracts reusable insights for transfer across heterogeneous tasks.
evidence: Evaluations on benchmark datasets (not named in the abstract); improves reasoning accuracy while reducing token overhead versus strong memory baselines, and knowledge distilled from fact verification enhances multi-hop reasoning.
not_tested: Code is not yet released so the method could not be independently verified, and the abstract does not state specific benchmark names, models, or headline numbers.
title: SEDM: Scalable Self-Evolving Distributed Memory for Agents

claim: Reconceptualizing prompt optimization as a collaborative multi-agent process, coordinated via semantic gradient embedding, conflict detection, and fusion, outperforms single-agent and random prompt optimization baselines.
method: MAPGD assigns specialized agents to distinct refinement dimensions (instruction clarity, example selection, format structure, stylistic adaptation) and coordinates their contributions via semantic gradient embedding, conflict detection, and fusion, adding two mechanisms: Hypersphere Constrained Gradient Clustering (HCGC) and Channel Adaptive Agent Weighting (CAAW).
evidence: Experiments on classification and reasoning benchmarks (not named in the abstract); MAPGD consistently surpasses single-agent and random baselines in accuracy and efficiency, with ablations confirming the effectiveness of gradient fusion, agent specialization, and conflict resolution.
not_tested: No interaction with a memory bank is studied, and the abstract does not give specific benchmark names, models, or headline numbers.
title: MAPGD: Multi-Agent Prompt Gradient Descent for Collaborative Prompt Optimization

claim: Semantically equivalent training prompts are not interchangeable during fine-tuning — they induce different cross-task effects on catastrophic forgetting and generalization — and superior prompts can be identified in advance via task loss and exploited through state-adaptive optimization.
method: State-Adaptive Prompt Optimization (SAPO), a lightweight training strategy that shifts task formulation from a static input to a dynamic, state-adaptive variable during fine-tuning.
evidence: Comprehensive experiments on diverse benchmarks (not named in the abstract); SAPO significantly mitigates forgetting while improving generalization, achieving substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art methods, and superior prompts are shown to be identifiable via task loss prior to learning.
not_tested: The abstract does not give specific benchmark names, models, or headline numbers, and no memory-bank or retrieval interaction is studied.
title: Training Prompt Matters: State-Adaptive Optimization for Robust Fine-Tuning

claim: Framing retrieval as a joint decoding problem over the whole corpus, via sparse non-negative reconstruction of the query embedding, can handle queries that standard dense (inner-product top-k) retrieval cannot, while never handling fewer queries than dense retrieval.
method: Non-Negative elastic Net (NNN) decoding selects a set of documents whose embeddings jointly reconstruct the query embedding as a sparse non-negative linear combination, applied both to frozen embeddings and via an end-to-end training procedure that optimizes embeddings specifically for NNN decoding.
evidence: A theoretical result establishes strict separation between dense retrieval and NNN decoding: every query dense retrieval handles correctly, NNN decoding also handles, and on corpora with correlated documents NNN decoding handles additional queries dense retrieval cannot. Experimentally, applying NNN decoding to frozen embeddings yields consistent improvements across several benchmarks, and end-to-end trained embeddings yield significant gains surpassing dense retrieval in all metrics and benchmarks (specific benchmark names and numbers not given in the abstract).
not_tested: The computational/scaling cost of corpus-aware joint decoding relative to per-query dense retrieval is not addressed, and the method is not tested in an LLM-agent memory setting (this is general information retrieval).
title: Non-negative Elastic Net Decoding for Information Retrieval

claim: Agentic RAG systems should be understood and designed as sequential decision-making systems, and the paper offers the first unified formalization, taxonomy, and risk analysis for them.
method: Formalizes agentic retrieval-generation loops as finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes and builds a modular taxonomy categorizing systems by planning mechanism, retrieval orchestration, memory paradigm, and tool-invocation behavior.
evidence: No empirical evaluation is reported; this is a Systematization of Knowledge (survey/formalization) paper with no models, benchmarks, or headline numbers.
not_tested: Does not empirically test any memory system, retrieval mechanism, or evaluation protocol; risks such as memory poisoning, hallucination propagation, and retrieval misalignment are identified conceptually but not measured.
title: SoK: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Taxonomy, Architectures, Evaluation, and Research Directions

claim: A proposed hybrid adaptive memory (HAM) system outperforms MemGPT and standard RAG baselines on long-context conversational task success across multiple real-world dialogue datasets.
method: HAM combines learned memory selection criteria with BM25 lexical matching and HNSW-based semantic retrieval, plus dynamic demonstration selection, adaptive memory gating, and 4-bit KV-cache quantization for resource-constrained serving.
evidence: Evaluated on >45K dialogue turns across Doc2Dial, PersonaChat, and MultiWOZ 2.4 against MemGPT, standard RAG, and retrieval-based context reconstruction baselines; HAM improves task success rate by 15.318% over vanilla RAG and 8.2-12.7% over MemGPT; error analysis attributes 67% of retrieval failures to temporal reasoning gaps and 23% to entity coreference ambiguity; ablations show +4.1% from dynamic demonstration selection and +3.8% from adaptive memory gating; 4-bit quantization preserves 94.3% of full-precision quality with 41% memory reduction under an 8GB GPU/200ms latency budget.
not_tested: No LLM backbone is identified for the compared systems, and no variance/statistical-significance reporting accompanies the headline percentage gains; generalization beyond the three chosen datasets and failure modes beyond the stated error taxonomy are not examined.
title: Memory-Augmented Retrieval for Long-Context Conversational AI: A Comparative Analysis of Adaptive Memory Mechanisms

claim: Memory management should be reframed as a sequential decision-making problem under uncertainty rather than governed by hand-designed heuristics, and the paper proposes DAM as a decision-theoretic framework for this reframing.
method: DAM decomposes memory management into immediate information access and hierarchical storage maintenance, evaluating candidate operations via value functions and uncertainty estimators arbitrated by an aggregate policy based on estimated long-term utility and risk.
evidence: No benchmarks, models, or headline numbers are given; the paper explicitly states its contribution is a conceptual/theoretical reframing rather than a new algorithm.
stated_limitations: not stated (paper explicitly frames itself as "not a new algorithm, but a principled reframing" providing "a foundation for future research," implying no empirical validation is offered)
not_tested: No experiments testing DAM's value functions or uncertainty estimators against heuristic memory-management baselines; no benchmarks, model backbones, or computational-cost measurements are reported.
title: Beyond Heuristics: A Decision-Theoretic Framework for Agent Memory Management

claim: HyperSkill, a hypergraph-structured skill memory framework that jointly handles storage, retrieval, and memory evolution, outperforms ten memory baselines on agentic benchmarks.
method: Represents memory as a hypergraph with subtask-step and skill nodes linked by hyperedges per trajectory; performs dual-path retrieval over subtask and trajectory levels ranking skills by co-occurrence, and periodically prunes low-utility nodes and merges redundant skills via quality-weighted propagation.
evidence: Evaluated on xBench, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA with GPT-4o and Qwen3-30B-A3B; outperforms ten memory baselines with gains up to +11.51 on GAIA and +11.18 on WebWalkerQA.
not_tested: No discussion of interaction with prompt optimization; no ablation isolating the effect of injection budget/number of retrieved items; no reported cost or latency overhead of hypergraph construction and maintenance.
title: HyperSkill: Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Hypergraph-Structured Skill Memory

claim: Integrating structured long-term memory with a memory-retrieval-driven reasoning module into a unified end-to-end cognitive loop improves long-horizon agent decision-making relative to short-term-state-reliant approaches.
method: Introduces a structured long-term memory mechanism for continuous storage and selective updating of cross-temporal information, coupled tightly with perception representation, reasoning, and policy generation in one cognitive loop.
evidence: "Comparative evaluations in open source interactive task settings" reportedly show consistent advantages in task completion quality, decision efficiency, and long-term information utilization; no specific benchmark names, baselines, model backbones, or headline numbers are given.
not_tested: No named benchmarks, baselines, or quantitative results are provided, so effect sizes and statistical reliability cannot be verified; no ablation separating the memory module's contribution from the reasoning module's; no test of scaling to longer horizons or cross-domain transfer.
title: Cognitive Modeling for Long-Horizon Agent Learning via Integrated Long-Term Memory and Reasoning

claim: Jointly meta-evolving an agent's experiential knowledge and its memory architecture (rather than using a static, manually engineered design) yields substantial performance gains and generalizes across tasks and backbone LLMs.
method: MemEvolve jointly evolves memory architecture and experiential knowledge; introduces EvolveLab, a unified codebase distilling twelve representative memory systems into a modular design space (encode, store, retrieve, manage) as a standardized substrate and fair experimental arena.
evidence: Evaluated on four agentic benchmarks; improves frameworks such as SmolAgent and Flash-Searcher by up to 17.06%, with demonstrated cross-task and cross-LLM generalization of the designed memory architectures.
not_tested: No per-baseline breakdown or statistical significance is given beyond the headline 17.06% figure; the computational/search cost of meta-evolution versus a fixed heuristic memory design is not discussed; interaction with prompt optimization is not addressed.
title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems

claim: Holistic competence in selecting, acting on, writing, and maintaining experience (not just retaining it) can be distilled via slow-fast co-evolution into a deployable policy, letting a small model (OPD-Evolver-9B) challenge much larger models.
method: A fast loop interacts with a four-level memory hierarchy (read, use, write, maintain) for rapid test-time evolution, while a slow loop uses outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight to distill these four abilities via on-policy self-distillation into the deployable policy.
evidence: Across multi-domain benchmarks, OPD-Evolver surpasses memory systems such as ReasoningBank by up to 11.5% and training-based methods such as Skill0 by ~5.8%; OPD-Evolver-9B is shown to challenge giant models such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash.
not_tested: No description of the retrieval injection budget (how many memory items are read/used per query); no reported variance or statistical testing for the headline percentage gains; no discussion of interaction with prompt optimization; generalization beyond the tested multi-domain benchmarks is not addressed.
title: OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation

claim: For reference-grounded QA evaluation, a prompt-controlled holistic LLM judge matches or exceeds a self-decomposing atomic judge on two of three benchmarks, indicating that atomic decomposition itself (rather than richer prompting) is not the main source of any atomic-judge advantage, with the holistic edge concentrated in detecting partial support.
method: Compares a self-decomposing atomic judge (single-prompt decompose-and-verify) against a prompt-controlled holistic judge given identical inputs and a similarly detailed rubric, classifying candidates as fully supported, partially supported, or unsupported relative to a reference.
evidence: 200 source examples per dataset across TruthfulQA, ASQA, and QAMPARI, four model families, source-level paired tests, cluster bootstrap, and aggregation across three pre-frozen prompt variants per design family; holistic judge favored on ASQA and QAMPARI (statistically reliable in three of four model families), atomic judge shows a small edge on TruthfulQA; a human-annotation sensitivity check confirms the ranking; reference-quality degradation produced the largest accuracy drops for both judge families.
stated_limitations: Our finding is specific to the self-decomposing single-prompt pattern on three QA-style benchmarks with 200 source examples each; multi-stage atomic pipelines and non-QA tasks remain untested.
not_tested: Multi-stage atomic pipelines and non-QA tasks (explicitly stated as untested); also does not test how judge design interacts with a memory system or with optimized instructions, nor larger sample sizes beyond 200 examples per dataset.
title: Rethinking Atomic Decomposition for LLM Judges: A Prompt-Controlled Study of Reference-Grounded QA Evaluation

claim: Current LLM agents can adapt locally within a task but rarely distill episodic experience into robust, reusable procedural skills.
method: SkillEvolBench, a 180-task diagnostic benchmark across six real-world agent environments with role-conditioned task families, has agents learn from acquisition tasks, update an external skill library from compacted trajectories and verifier feedback, and then face frozen deployment tasks testing context shift, adversarial shortcuts, and composition, comparing self-generated and curated-start skill evolution against no-skill and raw-trajectory controls.
evidence: Ten model configurations, three agent harnesses, six agent environments; raw-trajectory reuse frequently outperforms distilled skills, and capacity/cost analyses show writing more skills or larger Tier-3 libraries is not sufficient, introducing episode-specific drift and procedural clutter.
not_tested: Does not test whether alternative distillation/abstraction procedures could avoid discarding contextual cues, nor skill durability over longer horizons than the frozen deployment tasks studied.
title: SkillEvolBench: Benchmarking the Evolution from Episodic Experience to Procedural Skills

claim: Treating an agent's entire memory construction-retrieval (MCR) pipeline as an evolvable program, rather than only adapting the memory bank or prompt text, produces better long-horizon memory systems.
method: MemPro maintains a version tree of runnable MCR pipeline implementations, with an Evolving Agent iteratively selecting promising versions, diagnosing recurring failures, and producing improved child versions through failure-mode-guided edit-debug refinement.
evidence: Experiments on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, HotpotQA, and NarrativeQA show MemPro consistently outperforms strong static and prompt-level evolving baselines within a few iterations, continues improving with further evolution, and achieves a favorable performance-cost trade-off; no specific numeric deltas given.
not_tested: Does not test scaling to many more evolution iterations or long-term stability, nor generalization beyond the four QA/memory benchmarks used.
title: MemPro: Agentic Memory Systems as Evolvable Programs

claim: A runtime substrate that separates operation admission, information-flow admission, and durable causal evidence can let an agent's model-visible action surface (including persistent memory, skills, and tool synthesis) evolve after deployment without implicitly expanding resource authority or permitted information flows.
method: Agent libOS is an agent-native library OS with three planes (operation admission via identity/Task Authority ceilings/typed Capabilities/policy or human approval/budgets; information-flow admission via label propagation and Human-gated high-sensitivity egress; durable causal evidence recording), providing persistent processes, Object Memory, Skills, syscall-mediated JIT tools, images/checkpoints, typed providers, human queues, budgets, and durable recovery, with provider effects using a prepare-dispatch-settle protocol.
evidence: Source-bound evaluation: 33/33 deterministic full-runtime tasks pass both task and safety oracles; 12 canonical real-model runs achieve 12/12 observed safety and strict utility; a paired 30-run Skill projection study passes the observable-state oracle in all runs, with 13/15 fully correct runs in each arm.
stated_limitations: Agent libOS does not prevent prompt injection, provide kernel-grade sandboxing, or roll back irreversible external effects; results describe only the evaluated model/provider configuration.
not_tested: Does not test defenses against prompt injection, kernel-grade sandboxing, or rollback of irreversible external effects, and does not test generalization beyond the evaluated model/provider configuration.
title: Agent libOS: A Runtime Substrate for Capability-Controlled Self-Evolving LLM Agents

claim: Cross-episode procedural signals produced during RLVR rollouts can be distilled into reusable procedural memory and absorbed into a policy's weights during training, improving over episode-local self-distillation while yielding a memory-free model at inference.
method: Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD) extracts, online from the model's own trajectories, memory at three abstraction levels (raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies/lessons, and higher-level recurring behavioral patterns); a memory-conditioned self-teacher uses this accumulated memory to supervise the student on its own rollouts, with policy and memory co-evolving.
evidence: Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B: PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH; freezing either memory or policy trails full PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.
not_tested: Does not test model scales beyond 7-8B or benchmarks outside SCIKNOWEVAL/LIVECODEBENCH, and does not compare against non-parametric (retrieval-based) memory since PMD's memory is absorbed into weights and discarded at inference.
title: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models

claim: Recasting automatic prompt optimization as discrete compositional learning over a codebook of reusable, atomic instruction units ('instincts') outperforms monolithic, instance-blind prompt optimization.
method: Prompt Codebooks (PCO) organizes prompt-construction knowledge in a discrete codebook; an LLM-based encoder routes each input to a small per-instance subset of entries, a generator composes them into a prompt for the frozen target model, and a critic emits a structured verdict decomposed into per-variable textual gradients that jointly train the encoder, generator, and codebook under a language-valued min-max objective.
evidence: Six benchmarks on Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B: improves over zero-shot by up to +30.36 points, surpasses GEPA by +3.34 on HotpotQA and +1.11 in aggregate, and reduces deployed prompt length by up to 14.1x versus MIPROv2 and 3.0x versus GEPA using only K=16 instincts.
not_tested: Does not test scaling beyond 8B-parameter models or interaction with an external episodic memory bank, since the codebook operates at the instruction level rather than as task-episode memory.
title: Prompt Codebooks: Discrete Compositional Optimization for Language Model Instruction Refinement

claim: Comparing complete contrasting chain-of-thought traces from a failed attempt and a successful retry on the same input yields an optimization signal for prompt optimization that prior methods do not capture, improving over GEPA.
method: ContraPrompt uses dyadic reasoning trace analysis: an instrumented agentic retry loop automatically generates contrastive fail/succeed trace pairs (sharing model, input, and base prompt) without human annotation, and extracted rules are organized into an input-aware decision tree that routes instructions by observable input characteristics.
evidence: On four reasoning/compliance benchmarks, ContraPrompt outperforms GEPA on all four (+8.29pp HotPotQA, +2.21pp GDPR-Bench, +7.14pp GPQA Diamond, +0.74pp BBH); removing dyadic trace contrastivity causes a -16% relative average drop; on 53 EvalSet black-box optimization problems it beats GEPA on 11, ties on 41, loses on 1 at equal budget; on FiNER-139 it gains +7.77pp over baseline and +1.94pp over GEPA.
not_tested: Does not test whether the retry-generated contrastive data is biased by the specific model used to produce it, nor generalization to tasks lacking a natural retry-with-feedback structure beyond the benchmarks studied.
title: ContraPrompt: Contrastive Prompt Optimization via Dyadic Reasoning Trace Analysis

claim: No single memory substrate consistently dominates across operating regimes for memory-augmented agents, motivating regime-aware substrate routing.
method: A controlled harness evaluation compares memory substrates (dense and sparse indices, text records, structural stores, hierarchical stores, refinement-based memories, parametric updates, activation-compatible context mechanisms) across three backbone models and four benchmark suites, instrumenting 26 performance and efficiency metrics under a unified harness.
evidence: Three backbone models, four benchmark suites spanning user-centric QA and agent-centric decision-making; broad retrieval benefits long-context factual QA but can harm sequential decision-making by shifting attention from action-critical context, and substrates effective at moderate history lengths can become costly or brittle at longer horizons.
not_tested: Does not test a dynamic substrate-routing mechanism itself (only motivates it as a needed component), and code/full reproducibility materials are not yet available (to be released upon acceptance).
title: Harness the Memory: A Holistic Evaluation of Memory Substrates in Memory Agents

claim: Agent failures from conflicting retrieved memory mainly originate at the first decision point where the conflicting memory is adopted (entry), propagate and amplify with repeated exposure, and are rarely recovered from, producing a 'compliance trap' in which stronger agents suffer larger absolute damage.
method: The Entry-Propagation-Recovery (E-P-R) trajectory-level framework diagnoses where memory first changes an action, whether that change persists, and whether the agent can recover after diverging from a correct path; it is instantiated on WebArena and on MemTrapBench, a controlled benchmark built to isolate these phases.
evidence: On WebArena and MemTrapBench, conflicting memory induces similar compliance rates across models, but once agents comply their success rates collapse to a low floor, and stronger agents suffer larger absolute damage per compliance event since each event erases more baseline capability.
not_tested: Does not test mitigation or control policies for reducing entry-level compliance (only argues such policies are needed), nor whether the findings generalize beyond WebArena-style web-agent tasks to other agent domains.
title: The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory
